articles.title: Steve Rosenberg: Historic talks with Xi and Trump are a coup for Putin
articles.summary: Thursday's meeting between the leaders of US, China and Russia will give Vladimir Putin a big stage - but it does not bring him closer to winning the war in Ukraine.
articles.body:
But Thursday's mini summit of Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping already looks like a win for the Kremlin.

Think back to 2022. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine President Putin was an international pariah. Western leaders were determined to isolate him and his country over the war in Ukraine.

Fast forward to 2026: Vladimir Putin has secured an historic meeting in Shenzhen. For the first time in history, the leaders of China, Russia and the United States will sit down – just the three of them – for talks.

That puts Putin exactly where he wants to be: at the top table of global politics, rubbing shoulders with the leaders of the two great powers.

It allows him to boast that Western pressure on Russia has failed.

"We see such examples in the failed attempts to isolate our country, Russia, which has faced unprecedented sanctions pressure," Putin told a business forum of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation organisation.

That was followed by a meeting with Xi Jinping.

But the Kremlin says the "showstopper" event in Shenzhen will be Putin's trilateral with Xi and Trump.

It allows him to play global statesman, even as the Russian military continues to pound Ukrainian towns and cities, and the Kremlin continues to reject the idea of an unconditional, comprehensive ceasefire.

One short meeting is unlikely to reshape the world. But it's the optics that are key. The picture. The photo-op. Three leaders, three big powers, discussing big issues.

In a way, Vladimir Putin will use this meeting to send a holiday postcard to the rest of the world. Instead of "Wish you were here", he'll sign it: "Look: I'm here."

But what of those who are not at the table?

Among European leaders, and especially in Ukraine, there is concern that the three-way meeting might produce more than just a pretty picture, though not in a good way for Kyiv.

Donald Trump has already said that in Shenzhen he wants to discuss his "favourite subject" - the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin would likely welcome an opportunity to argue its case to Trump and Xi without Ukrainian officials or European leaders in the room.

Last month Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed concern that the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting might resemble the Yalta Conference of 1945. That is when the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States – Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt - met to re-organise post-World War Two Europe.

"We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," said Zelensky.

It is unclear whether China would want the Ukraine war on the agenda in Shenzhen. In its official statements on the upcoming trilateral meeting, Beijing has talked more generally about the need to discuss "safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability".

In Shenzhen, Russia will make the most of the optics. But a diplomatic victory is not the same as a military one.

Nearly five years after President Putin launched his so-called "special military operation", Russia is still struggling to win its war on Ukraine.

Over this time, it has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.

And the Ukrainian strike on the road bridge linking Russia to the Crimean Peninsula – carried out on the eve of the summit - was a blow to Moscow's prestige. The attack severely damaged part of the multi-billion-dollar bridge built by Russia after it annexed Crimea from Ukraine.

The damage is not only a logistical headache for the Russian authorities.

It is a reminder that the Kremlin's "special operation" has not gone at all to plan.

The Shenzhen summit may give Vladimir Putin a big stage, and a bright spotlight.

It does not necessarily bring him closer to winning the war.

articles.title: Bomb blasts, arson rock Bangladesh ahead of Hasina's planned return; paramilitary deployed
articles.summary: Bangladesh stepped up security and deployed hundreds of paramilitary troops across the country on Wednesday as protests over the planned return of ousted
articles.body: Bangladesh stepped up security and deployed hundreds of paramilitary troops across the country on Wednesday as protests over the planned return of ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina triggered clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks allegedly carried out by supporters of her banned Awami League party.A petrol bomb killed a political activist in Hasina's hometown of Gopalganj, police said on Wednesday, as violence spread weeks ahead of her proposed return to the country.Hasina, 79, has been living in exile in neighbouring India since fleeing Dhaka in August 2024 following violent protests demanding her resignation. She has requested a new passport and identity card, saying she plans to return to Bangladesh in December. However, the government has so far rejected her request, prompting members and supporters of her Awami League party to stage protests.Last week, the party announced a week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support for Hasina's return, culminating in a nationwide lockdown on November 19.Police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of vehicles being set on fire across at least 28 districts over the past 10 days, with several police personnel and civilians injured, local media reported.Bomb blasts and arson attacksLate on Tuesday, an activist of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) was allegedly killed by unidentified attackers during a protest in Gopalganj, police said.On the same night, a crude bomb exploded outside the Dhaka residence of Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury. The house of a BNP lawmaker and shops belonging to BNP supporters in Gopalganj were also set on fire, police added.On Wednesday morning, a helper working for a bus company was burnt to death in the southern district of Pirojpur after two buses were set ablaze, authorities said.The violence comes a year after a local court sentenced Hasina to death in absentia after finding her guilty of ordering a deadly crackdown on the student-led uprising in 2024. She was convicted of crimes against humanity over the crackdown.Government blames Awami League leaders abroadAt least 37 branches and offices of Grameen Bank have been targeted in arson attacks or attempted fires since November 10, the bank said. Fourteen more were attacked after midnight on Tuesday.The bank was founded by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, who led Bangladesh's interim government following Hasina's ouster and has faced hostility from her supporters.Dhaka Metropolitan Police have arrested at least 71 members of banned organisations, including the Awami League and its affiliated groups, over the past 24 hours, police spokesperson Niaz Mehedi said.On Tuesday, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed accused Awami League leaders based abroad of inciting supporters to destabilise the country and set fire to property. He said those involved in the violence would be identified and prosecuted.Hasina has reiterated her intention to return to Bangladesh in December, reviving hopes among her supporters despite her conviction and death sentence.You use AI every day. articles.title: A year after picking up the gun: The end of Kashmir’s last known active LeT terrorist Lateef Bhat
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: On November 18, 2025, Mohammad Lateef Bhat joined Lashkar-e-Taiba, according to police.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: On November 18, 2025, Mohammad Lateef Bhat joined Lashkar-e-Taiba, according to police. Exactly a year later, he was killed in a gunfight in his home district of Kulgam. In between, the ‘A-category’ terrorist had become one of Kashmir’s most wanted, with a Rs 15 lakh bounty on his head. Police said he had been tasked with disrupting peace and damaging the Valley’s economy.‘A’ grade terroristCategorised as an ‘A’ category operative, Bhat was one of the most wanted local terrorists in Kashmir. He had been linked to two attacks in July this year.Officials described Bhat as a former carpenter who finished his Class 12 in 2021 and then dropped out of college in the early days.In November 2025, he went missing and joined LeT and its offshoot, The Resistance Front (TRF), officials said.On July 22, he allegedly shot dead Jammu and Kashmir Police head constable Ashiq Hussain in a crowded market area at Lal Chowk in Anantnag. On July 31, he was reportedly involved in the murder of two migrant workers from Chhattisgarh at a brick kiln in Kulgam.Law enforcement agencies subsequently identified him from CCTV screen grabs of the Lal Chowk area that captured the cop’s murder. In August, the Jammu and Kashmir Police announced a reward of Rs 15 lakh for information leading to him and put up his posters across prominent places in Kashmir.The banner appealed to people to provide credible information about the terrorists’ movements or whereabouts. It assured them that the identity of informants would remain confidential and that a reward would be given for reliable information.The search continued over the following months. On November 8, a banner seeking information about four wanted terrorists surfaced at Pratap Park in Srinagar’s Lal Chowk area. Bhat was named on it, along with Bilal Ahmad Mir, Mohammad Umar Mir and Abid Qayoom Lone, all from Baramulla district. Bhat was believed to be active in the Kashmir Valley, while the other three were suspected of operating from Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir, officials said."After joining the banned organisation Lashkar-e-Taiba, he was receiving directions from across (the border) to disrupt peace here, hit tourism, and damage the economy,” Kulgam senior superintendent of Police Anayat Ali Choudhary said.You have all seen his three or four attacks and how ruthlessly he carried them out," he added, as per ANI.Nail in the coffinOn November 11, Bhat and his associate Umar Nisar Dar opened fire on a Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) checkpoint in the Akhran area near Mir Bazar in Kulgam district, injuring three personnel. The attack took place at around 2.15 pm when two terrorists approached the checkpoint, which was manned by personnel of the CRPF's 46th Battalion.According to investigators, the attackers approached from a cluster of trees and dense vegetation. One of them opened indiscriminate fire with an AK-series rifle, while the other remained positioned on the road, providing cover. The CRPF personnel retaliated, forcing the attackers to flee through the surrounding vegetation.Investigators subsequently identified the attackers through CCTV footage that captured their movements during reconnaissance of potential targets in Mir Bazar, Akhran, Hablish and Killam on November 10, a day before the attack.The hunt that followed reached a turning point on Monday, when a gunfight broke out in the Larnoo area, around 100km south of Srinagar. Drones were deployed to scan the vast apple orchards and adjoining forests as security forces continued combing the area.Dar, was killed in that encounter. Bhat was also injured but managed to escape. He took shelter in a mosque located around 2-3 km away, having slipped away from the site of the earlier encounter near the Laru bypass.Police also suspected that Dar had been providing shelter and logistical assistance to Bhat for several months.Operation ZungalporaEarly Wednesday, security forces received specific intelligence inputs about Bhat’s location. The Jammu and Kashmir Police, CRPF and Army jointly launched a cordon-and-search operation around a mosque in Kulgam’s Zangalpora village after re-establishing contact with him.SSP Choudhary said the operation was carried out with careful planning and coordination among the security forces. Personnel made repeated attempts to persuade Bhat to surrender, including through a video call in which Choudhary personally spoke to him for an extended period.“We tried hard to persuade him to surrender, telling him that he is still young and has his whole life ahead of him. He did not agree and entered a mosque and opened fire around 2.45am,” Choudhary said.Security forces also made repeated announcements asking Bhat to surrender after he took shelter inside the mosque. He then opened fire on security personnel, triggering a gunfight.Because the mosque was within the cordoned-off area and Bhat was firing from inside it, Choudhary said, forces exercised maximum restraint. articles.title: Saudi coalition hits 60 Houthi military sites; Taiz sees ‘fierce battles’
articles.summary: Houthis advance towards Aden as Saudi-led coalition conducts precision strikes on key military targets in Yemen.
articles.body:
Saudi-led coalition forces have carried out a “precision operation” in Yemen against 60 Houthi military targets and destroyed tunnels used by the armed group as workshops and storage for ballistic missiles, according to the coalition’s spokesman.

Turki al-Maliki said on Wednesday morning that the strikes came in the governorates of Sanaa, Hodeidah, Amran and Saada on Tuesday during an advance by the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), towards the southern city of Aden, the temporary capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

In recent days, the Yemeni army and forces loyal to it withdrew from Dhubab airport and territory around the Bab-al-Mandeb strait, the strategic maritime chokepoint in western Taiz governorate, to defend Aden.

Elsewhere in Yemen, fighting resumed between the government forces and the Houthis in Tur al-Bahah in Lahij province.

Al Jazeera’s Hadeel al-Yamani, who is in Taiz, said “on the ground, fierce battles have been taking place between government forces and the Houthi group”.

“Local authorities accuse the Houthi group of shelling civilians and residential neighbourhoods,” al-Yamani said.

“These villages in Jabal Sabr are under a complete siege. There are urgent appeals for safe corridors to be opened for civilians, and daily sniper attacks [are] targeting civilians. People are being killed and injured, primarily children and women,” al-Yamani added.

Houthis accused of blocking medical supplies into Taiz

Taiz authorities accused Houthis of establishing checkpoints to impose levies on civilians and confiscating shipments of medicines and medical supplies that lacked licences from Yemen’s Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa.

In a statement published on Monday, Taiz’s Public Health and Population Office condemned the Houthis, saying “this escalatory move constitutes a direct assault on pharmaceutical security and a violation of the human right to access medicine and medical treatment”.

Taiz officials called on the United Nations to intervene, adding that Houthis were blocking the entry of medical supplies coming from Aden to Taiz, intensifying the ongoing siege and endangering “the lives of thousands of patients whose continued treatment” is at risk.

Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two cruise missiles launched by Houthis towards the capital, Riyadh, on Wednesday. The attacks are the latest in weeks of strikes by the Yemeni armed group targeting Saudi military, civilian and oil infrastructure.

The Houthis’ military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said the group targeted oil pumping stations near Riyadh and a radar installation in southern Saudi Arabia.

Saudi authorities have so far not responded to the claims.

Alerts were sounded in the Saudi cities of Jizan, Najran and Khamis Mushait on Wednesday before the danger passed.

articles.title: ‘Partnership buys silence’: Fears grow over EU-Rwanda deportation plans
articles.summary: A British immigration lawyer, Rwandan journalist, rights groups and leading politicians decry the proposal as inhumane.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – The seven asylum seekers were on the runway, their plane bound for Rwanda from a military airport in southern England.

They were being sent thousands of kilometres away to a country they had never visited and with little idea of what awaited them.

But after much legal wrangling, a ruling from the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) stopped their deportation minutes before the flight was due to take off.

British immigration lawyer Alasdair Mackenzie, who was involved in the case, said the people being deported – among them Iranians, Iraqis, an Albanian and a Vietnamese citizen – were terrified.

“A lot of them were in an absolutely desperate state,” he told Al Jazeera. “They felt terrified as they were going to a place they didn’t know, being shunted around like packages. Rwanda is a very repressive country. There were concerns that asylum seekers would not be able to speak up or protest about their conditions.”

Four years later, European governments are preparing to revive the idea.

Germany, Denmark, Greece, Austria and the Netherlands announced plans on Monday to establish a deportation centre in Rwanda for people whose asylum claims have been rejected. The proposal is part of a wider European push to increase removals by transferring rejected asylum seekers to “return hubs” in countries with which they have no previous connection.

Rwanda has pledged independent monitoring and the involvement of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. It has also pushed back against concerns from rights groups. On Tuesday, after 47 organisations decried the proposal and warned that Rwanda does not respect international human rights standards, Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said: “Human rights in Rwanda are respected and granted to everyone and specifically to refugees who choose to come to our country.”

Rwandan investigative journalist Samuel Baker Byansi, who now lives in an undisclosed location in Europe, said of the new plans: “This partnership buys their silence.”

In 2022, Byansi was investigating Rwanda’s suspected military activities in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) with his colleague John Williams Ntwali. He said he received warnings that they both could be arrested or killed.

“I received a tip from credible sources that me and my colleagues would be subject of arrest or elimination. I had a way to leave the country, so I did. John died months later,” he told Al Jazeera.

Ntwali officially died in a reported road accident, but Byansi and human rights monitors have questioned the circumstances surrounding his death.

Byansi fears the migration deal will give the Rwandan government another way to deflect international scrutiny.

President Paul “Kagame puts Western governments in a position where they cannot hold him accountable.”

Kagame, Rwanda’s leader since 2000, has been praised for overseeing the country’s economic transformation after the 1994 genocide. But his government faces persistent accusations of repression.

The UN and other organisations have repeatedly accused Rwanda of supporting the armed group M23 in its war in the eastern DRC. In October, the United States announced sanctions against Rwanda’s Ministry of Defence over its “destabilising activities”.

In October, a prominent critic of the Rwandan government was found decapitated outside the Ugandan capital, Kampala.

Amnesty International argued that transferring asylum seekers and migrants to a country with such a record risks leaving them with little protection or ability to challenge their treatment.

“Sending people to a country they have never been to is irresponsible, and there is a real danger that the Rwanda deal will, with its limited chance for scrutiny, become a cruel black hole for human rights,” the rights group said.

Some are concerned about the potential to monitor the treatment of people after they are deported.

Tineke Strik, a Dutch member of the European Parliament, visited Rwanda in September to inspect facilities in Kigali that could be used to house Europe’s rejected asylum seekers.

Rwandan officials presented the proposal as a mutually beneficial arrangement, telling her the people who arrive could remain in the country and eventually receive residency or citizenship.

“The authorities were pitching the scheme as a win-win,” Strik told Al Jazeera. “… But it was not possible for us to verify their claims as there are no [domestic] NGOs expressing criticism.”

Strik also tried to establish the whereabouts and wellbeing of people recently deported to Rwanda by United States President Donald Trump’s administration but was unable to obtain details.

“It made me convinced how impossible it will be for European governments to check on what is happening over there.”

Rwanda has previously been used as a destination for deported asylum seekers. From 2013 to 2018, Israel sent thousands of Eritrean and Sudanese citizens to the country. Many reportedly subsequently left Rwanda or were deported elsewhere.

The United Kingdom’s proposed arrangement with Kigali in 2022 accumulated estimated costs of $940m but resulted in just four voluntary transfers before the Supreme Court ruled it unlawful. The Labour government abandoned it in 2024, the same year the party won a general election and returned to power.

The European proposals would apply to people whose asylum claims have been rejected, rather than potentially all unauthorised arrivals.

But lawyers involved in the earlier British scheme remain concerned about the consequences of sending people to a country where they may struggle to challenge their treatment.

In 2018, Rwandan police fired on several Congolese refugees protesting against food cuts in the country’s west. Twelve died in an incident that has added to concerns about the protection available to vulnerable refugees and migrants already living there.

Kigali has nevertheless defended its role as a potential destination for deported asylum seekers and migrants.

Rwanda hosts large numbers of refugees, predominantly from neighbouring DRC and Burundi. Interior Minister Biruta described Rwanda’s policies as “progressive” because they allow people to work and launch businesses.

Dissent from Spain’s Sanchez to a Dutch politician: Deal ‘will not work’

The proposals have also exposed divisions within Europe over how far governments should go to deter irregular migration.

While Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner defended the initiative as “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the scheme has no “future or humanity”. French President Emmanuel Macron questioned the idea in June. “I’m not sure that these are the fundamental principles on which our Europe was built, and I don’t believe it’s effective either,” he said.

Asylum applications in the European Union lodged in the first half of 2026 fell by 17 percent compared with the same period a year earlier, reaching their lowest level since 2021.

“Europe could invest much more in establishing a smoother cooperation with countries of origin,” Strik said. Return hubs are expensive, apply to few people, carry a high reputational risk “and will not work”, she said.

Further details of the Rwanda scheme are expected in early 2027, and an initial pilot project at this point is expected to involve about 100 people.

Aside from the human rights concerns, Mackenzie, the immigration lawyer, questioned the theory that return hubs would act as a deterrent.

“People don’t set off and cover thousands of miles across land and sea with the expectation that they are going to be sent back. To the extent that they are aware of these policies, they are prepared to take the risk because the economic or political conditions in their home countries are so dire.”

articles.title: The anti-Israel left is escalating its demands — and the threat to Jews has never been more dangerous
articles.summary: Ro Khanna demanded zero aid to Israel at the Democrats' "What's Next" conference, a 2028 litmus test DSA allies hope Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez will embrace.
articles.body: Much like "justice" and "accountability," few words are more beloved by anti-Israel activists and agitators than "escalation." "Escalate protests to an open Intifada in every capital and city," cried a coalition of pro-Palestinian groups back in May 2024, as the first volley of #freegaza rallies and encampments upended colleges and city centers across the globe. "Unapologetically extreme" is what the Anti-Defamation League called anti-Zionist groups, such as the self-described "Escalate Network," in a report from the same period detailing escalation strategies being planned for students returning to schools that autumn. "Escalate BDS pressure to end all state, corporate and institutional complicity in Israel’s illegal occupation, apartheid and genocide," cried a coalition of Palestinian trade unions and Boycott Divestment Sanctions (BDS) groups earlier this month. OBAMA, HARRIS LEAN INTO 'GAZAMAXXING' AS BLACK VOTERS FOCUS ON AMERICA FOR THE MIDTERMS — NOT THE MIDEAST But even for a movement defined by years of incitement and provocation, anti-Israel politicians and activists are now calling for a level of escalation whose potential for menace — and yes, violence — feels almost limitless. Take Darializa Avila Chevalier, the newly elected Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) congresswoman from New York. On election day two weeks back — mere hours after President Trump announced an end to military support for Israel — Chevalier made clear in a post on X that Trump’s historic pull-back should just be the beginning. "Military aid is not enough. We need to end U.S. taxpayer funding for Israel’s war crimes, a full arms embargo, and the Palestinian right of return." Chevalier is hardly the only congressional newcomer — or DSA member — to make such a brazen and unprecedented demand. Just a few months earlier, the incoming Colorado Rep. Melat Kiros also suggested Palestinians be given the "right of return" to the homes they left following Israel’s independence in 1948. Missing from Kiros’ missive was any acknowledgment that those homes — or at least the land they once stood upon — almost certainly now belong to Jewish Israelis. Nor have Kiros and Chevalier – along with fellow right-of-returner author Ta-Nehisi Coates — acknowledged that the properties were abandoned both as a consequence of a multilateral diplomatic process and often (in towns such as Haifa and Jaffa) at the urging of the local Arab leadership. Or that until the organized, Soviet-backed Palestinian liberation struggle emerged during the 1960s, the word 'Palestinian' often referred to the Jews —and not just Arabs — living in the historic and colonial lands known then as ‘Palestine,’ under the control of the British mandate. Yet rather than merely settle for a "right to return," Kiros is escalating her anti-Zionist demands even further. She wants Israel — a nation intimately familiar with the history of reparations — to itself pay reparations to Arabs for land lost during Israel’s establishment back in 1948. Kiros is far from alone in suggesting that Palestinians be compensated for their decades of political missteps and malfeasance. In her new book, "Confronting Zionism: Decolonizing Palestine and Building the World Anew," Rutgers University professor Noura Erakat has also called for reparations — along with a right-to-return. Hardly surprising from a woman who’s cast doubt on Hamas’ use of mass-rape on Oct. 7 and has also insisted that Hamas – despite clear documentation from organizations such as the NATO Center of Excellence for Strategic Communications — has never deployed civilians as human shields. NYC DSA URGES AOC TO RUN FOR PRESIDENT WHILE PLANNING TO TAKE OVER CITY COUNCIL Such fabulism would be easy to dismiss if it weren’t now accompanied by the potential to become political policy. But the escalations today have shifted from mere protests and social media posts straight to the 2028 presidential race. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER Last week, at the Democrats’ highly-consequential "What’s Next" conference in Colorado, Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., declared: "Reject AIPAC. Zero aid to Israel. Zero weapons to Israel. The next president must say no more foreign wars. None." These are litmus-tests-in-the-making almost certain to be echoed by every potential Democratic presidential candidate — particularly Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., now being pushed by her DSA comrades to run for the White House. Never mind that the DSA’s rabidly anti-Israel agenda sits at odds with the centrist policies that propelled the Democrats’ midterm sweep. Buoyed by its handful of wins, the DSA is mulling a comprehensive anti-Israel escalation plan to not merely weaken U.S. support for the Jewish state, but "break" Israel’s historic alliance with Washington. The proposed highlights include blocking Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., respective speakerships — along with potentially targeting United Airlines flights to Tel Aviv, which the DSA claims are used to transport weaponry to Israel. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Beyond such theatrics — which are likely to generate far more headlines than actual results — are the graver and unspoken implications of escalations like reparations and the right of return. The specter of the former, for instance, layers U.S.-styled racial dynamics onto the already fraught — and ethnically-complex — Israeli-Palestinian conflict. One look at the damage this type of identity politicking has wrought upon America should serve as a warning to Israel to end any reparations debates before they begin. Talk of a right-of-return, meanwhile, raises the possibility of mass Jewish expulsion from Israel — the Jewish nation. Or a "one-state" solution where Jews would almost certainly become a minority. Or, perhaps, something even far more sinister. Don’t forget, Coates himself has repeatedly suggested that had he been born a Palestinian in Gaza, he might not have had the "strength" to resist joining in the Hamas horrors of Oct. 7. And whether it is Israelis shot dead in Washington, D.C., or a Yom Kippur attack on a synagogue in Manchester or a Hanukkah beachside massacre in Australia, the blood being shed is almost inevitably Jewish.

articles.title: Palestinians find refuge in ancient caves after Israel demolishes homes
articles.summary: Palestinians displaced in the occupied West Bank’s Masafer Yatta area have been forced to live in underground caves.
articles.body:
Masafer Yatta, occupied West Bank – Mohamad Dababseh, 60, spent several days trying to clear water from the cave he now calls his home after last week’s storm.

The flooding happened after the Israeli army demolished part of the cave, claiming it was an unauthorised dwelling, and allowed water to seep into his home.

Mohamad and his family of 12 were forced to sleep in tents after their home was demolished for the sixth time. They lacked the funds to rebuild, as he had managed to do on previous occasions. The Israeli army even demolished and confiscated the tents, leaving the residents with no choice but to sleep under the trees throughout the summer of 2025.

The ancient underground caves, for which Masafer Yatta is known, became the residents’ last resort, despite being unsuitable for habitation. They are damp and poorly ventilated, but the Israeli army has continued its campaign of harassment against locals by demolishing parts of their cave dwellings as well.

“My wife and I have developed respiratory problems due to the high humidity inside the cave. In the winter, our suffering intensifies as water seeps in, flooding the floor and damaging our belongings,” Mohamad told Al Jazeera.

For most residents of Khallet al-Daba, a village in the Masafer Yatta area south of Hebron, living in caves was not a choice. They were forced to find shelter in these nearby caves after the Israeli army demolished their homes and shelters more than six times, reducing most of their villages to ruins.

For decades, Masafer Yatta, home to nearly 2,000 Palestinians, has seen a steadily suffocating Israeli campaign aimed at seizing their land. Israel’s campaign includes the demolition of homes, many of which have stood for more than 70 years, and the confiscation of livestock, the primary source of income for residents.

The assault on the region escalated in 1980, when Israel declared more than 35,000 dunams (35sq km) of Masafer Yatta a “closed military zone”, despite the presence of 12 Palestinian communities in the area. Israel subsequently began establishing illegal settlements on the land, effectively seizing territory from the Palestinians.

The campaign against the Palestinians in Masafer Yatta continues to this day. On October 20, the Israeli army demolished a portion of the cave where the Dababseh family reside, citing renovations he had carried out to make it slightly more habitable. Having lost his only source of income, Mohamad is no longer able to repair it. Instead, fellow villagers have provided some materials to help him fix parts of it.

“Every time my home was demolished, I would sell some of my livestock to rebuild it until I realised that, due to the repeated demolitions, I no longer had any livestock left to sell. Now, I live in a cave with my family, unable to repair it after parts of it were torn down,” said Mohamad.

Jaber Dababseh, who is also a spokesperson for the residents of Khallet al-Daba, said 100 of 120 residents of the village have sought shelter in caves. Only two families remain in their homes, which are also at risk of demolition at any moment.

“The underground cave is not adequately equipped for a school student; there is neither sufficient lighting nor ventilation. Furthermore, the children cannot freely enjoy their simple right to play, given how difficult the space is. Yet, they have grown accustomed to these harsh conditions ever since our home began to be demolished time and time again,” he told Al Jazeera.

“The residents are trying to adapt to this imposed reality, so they don’t have to leave Masafer Yatta. It is another form of resilience they have devised to challenge their difficult circumstances.”

It is almost impossible to pipe water into the caves, so residents rely on storage tanks, which are frequently sabotaged by Israeli soldiers and settlers. Electricity is a distant dream, so they make do with solar-powered lamps.

With no alternative, Jaber’s three children, aged between three and 15, have been forced to adapt to the new environment.

“When we want to repair or reinforce the caves, we do it at night, so the Israeli army doesn’t see us,” he explained. “Sometimes, they raid the caves to inspect them; if they find signs of repairs, they issue orders to demolish any structures inside.”

Following Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023, settler attacks across Masafer Yatta intensified, coinciding with an escalating campaign of demolitions targeting Palestinian homes and animal enclosures.

Since 2023, settlers have established 13 new illegal outposts in Masafer Yatta, declared “military zones”, with an additional nine outposts set up outside these areas.

In a statement issued on September 24, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said three villages in the area were almost entirely destroyed that month.

In May 2025, the Israeli army carried out its largest demolition operation in Khallet al-Daba, destroying every dwelling in the village.

The operation included homes, agricultural facilities, water tanks and solar panels. The OHCHR warned of the dire consequences resulting from these demolitions and the forced displacement of the area’s residents.

Nidal Younis, head of the Masafer Yatta Village Council, told Al Jazeera that more than 40 families from various villages in Masafer Yatta have returned to these ancient caves. These are deeply rooted in the region’s history, some dating back to the Canaanite and Roman eras.

They have been used as temporary refuges for residents in the area over the centuries and have become an integral part of local Palestinian culture. After residents moved into fixed stone homes, they were used for farmers’ livestock.

The return of locals to these caves reflects a harsh decline in living conditions, according to Younis, following Israeli restrictions and demolitions of their homes.

“The caves in Masafer Yatta were once part of the traditional way of life for the region’s inhabitants, but today they are considered extremely primitive dwellings, lacking any of the features of a standard home,” he said.

“The difficulty of providing water and electricity, the absence of sewage systems, and the structural weakness exacerbated by a ban on renovations, all combine to further the suffering of those who live there.”

Younis said the suffering the residents continue to endure extends beyond the demolition of homes and the confiscation of property.

Water, the most essential resource for survival, has been targeted regularly in the village, with pipes destroyed, tankers barred from entering the area, and wells for rainwater collection seized. Securing water for residents is now a daily challenge, with 12 villages in Masafer Yatta without any stock or supply.

Israeli authorities have also targeted small solar panels residents use to generate limited power, while over the past two months, 13 vehicles and agricultural tractors have been confiscated, with huge sums of money demanded for their return.

“These attacks are a part of a broader effort to isolate Masafer Yatta from its Palestinian surroundings and compel its residents to leave,” Younis said. “Yet, the locals continue to seek alternatives that will allow them to remain in their villages.”

articles.title: Russell Brand: Deputy Labour leader criticises media for 'amplifying' prison message
articles.summary: Lucy Powell says outlets shouldn't have played a clip of a message read by the jailed rapist's wife.
articles.body:
Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell has criticised media organisations for broadcasting a message from the wife of jailed rapist Russell Brand on his behalf.

Laura Brand read out the message on the disgraced comedian's YouTube channel on Sunday, in which he said he was not guilty of the offences for which he is serving a 10-and-a-half year prison sentence .

The message has prompted an official investigation into whether Brand broke prison rules.

The clip of Laura Brand has been played on outlets including BBC Radio 4's Today programme, ITV's This Morning, Sky News, LBC and the News Agents podcast. On Wednesday, Education Secretary Powell said the media should not have "amplified" his words.

"I was appalled at that [message] and actually I think mainstream media shouldn't have transmitted that either," she told LBC on Wednesday.

"It's a platform I don't think should have been amplified, to be honest."

Powell went on to describe Russell Brand as "someone who's not showing a jot of remorse, a jot of any sensitivity at all to their victims".

She continued: "This is somebody who's been convicted and found guilty of very, very serious offences and rape."

In a statement, the BBC said the Today programme had played the Laura Brand clip "in error, due to miscommunication within the team", and had since removed it from catch-up service BBC Sounds.

BBC News has asked the other outlets named above for a comment.

ITN News chief executive Ian Rumsey told BBC Radio 4's The Media Show that the company's newsrooms, including ITV News and Channel 4 News, took the decision not to play the video.

He said: "You didn't need to show it. You could discuss, you could describe what it was, and I'm very pleased and proud that every area of ITN chose not to show it at all, and I think that's exactly the right decision."

YouTube said it is aware of the video and investigating, and that Brand's channel on the platform hasn't been able to make money since being suspended from its advert revenue scheme for "violating" its "creator responsibility policy" after allegations against him emerged in 2023. But the channel is still available to view.

Brand's social media accounts on Meta platforms - which owns Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - were disabled last week.

Earlier this week, Downing Street officials described Brand's message to his followers as "clearly appalling", adding that it was being urgently investigated.

No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.

Asked about the message, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.

"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."

articles.title: Xi embraces Trump ahead of historic summit and experts explain the recent tech outages: Morning Rundown
articles.summary: Cybersecurity experts say the series of recent outages aren’t an attack.
articles.body: Cybersecurity experts say the series of recent outages aren’t an attack. In a rare move, President Xi greets Trump as he lands in China. And could a new Netflix show be the streaming service’s answer to YouTube. Here’s what to know today. Why so many major computer systems went down in a week An unusual string of tech outages continued yesterday, with Apple, the National Weather Service and Marriott reporting problems. In addition, a key classified National Security Agency network stopped working for several hours, though there was no indication it was caused by an attack. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. Ordinarily, the pauses in service might have escaped scrutiny. But they’re the latest in a wave of outages that has affected services affecting everyday life, including Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration and Chase Bank. President Donald Trump brushed off concerns, saying yesterday, “It’s life, it’s life.” He added: “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.” The reassurances have not calmed tensions even within his own coalition. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who has refused to apologize or accept responsibility for the FAA outage, is now demanding $50 billion in new funding. He was “yelled at” during a contentious closed-door briefing yesterday with Senate Republicans, a source said. Still, despite widespread speculation that something nefarious was afoot, cybersecurity experts say the public evidence behind the outages points to something more mundane: ordinary technological failures. They’re a natural result of society becoming increasingly reliant on computer systems for key functions, one expert said. But the companies behind the systems “are operating in a system of misaligned market forces,” in which they’re “prioritizing speed and features, and they’re not competing on safety,” another expert said. Read the full story here. A handshake, and then a quick embrace with China’s president President Donald Trump arrived in China today ahead of high-stakes talks with his Chinese and Russian counterparts to discuss nuclear disarmament and the Iran war. Chinese President Xi greeted Trump as he walked off Air Force One, an extremely rare move that will likely be taken as a compliment by U.S. leader. The tarmac embrace is believed to be the first time the Chinese leader has been on hand to greet any American president arriving in the country. Russian President Vladimir Putin said he had high hopes for his meeting with Trump and Xi. “I expect great potential benefits from the upcoming trilateral meeting,” he said at the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, according to the Kremlin. Putin then had a bilateral talk with Xi, which lasted over two hours, according to Russian state news agency Tass. Trump also said he might also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, though Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there wasn’t a meeting scheduled between the two leaders. Trump’s trip to China followed a visit to the Philippines, where he announced at a state lunch that the two countries had reached a “very big trade deal” without providing details about the agreement. Follow our live blog for updates. Democrat Mary Peltola flips Alaska Senate seat Democrats extended their Senate majority in the 2026 election, with the victory of Mary Peltola in Alaska giving the party 56 seat total next year. Peltola defeated GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, marking the end of a race that had been roiled by allegations of ballot stacking and an accused spoiler candidate who was also named Dan Sullivan. Democrats ultimately flipped nine seats in this year’s elections, all but one in states Trump carried in 2024, leaving the Republicans with 44. A look back at the dramatic Senate race. More politics news: The White House pulled Dr. Heidi Overton’s nomination to lead the FDA after weeks of counts from key Republicans. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is calling for lowering the Medicare eligibility age, expanding benefits and offering universal health coverage for children. Nvidia enters the post-Jensen Huang era with a bang Nvidia’s third-quarter earnings of $115.8 billion exceeded expectations of AI chip sales, as the company’s leaders sought to assure investors that ousted CEO Jensen Huang will not be returning. Nvidia also raised its forecast for future sales to 75% of revenue growth, up from 70%, according to interim CEO Colette Kreiss. The company ended the day with its stock up 5%. Just hours before yesterday’s earnings release, Huang said he would be “honored” to return to the job of CEO, but Kreiss and newly elected board chair Harvey Jones quickly shot down the idea. Kreiss also answered questions about AI development ahead of Democratic majorities in Congress and the Senate, and whether there were worries about the Commerce Department restricting sales of advanced AI chips to several countries. Here’s what we learned. Related coverage: For subscribers: Trump had a mutually beneficial relationship with Huang and now seems reluctant to let it go. Staff Pick: Could a viral teen comedy be Netflix’s answer to YouTube? articles.title: 'Five defining features': Jaishankar decodes the changing world order
articles.summary: The global economy is increasingly being weaponised, with countries using access to energy, technology, finance and trade as tools of geopolitical
articles.body: The global economy is increasingly being weaponised, with countries using access to energy, technology, finance and trade as tools of geopolitical pressure, External affairs minister S Jaishankar warned on Wednesday, flagging five defining features reshaping the international order.Addressing the inaugural session of Raisina Tokyo 2026 in Japan, Jaishankar said repeated global shocks, strategic competition and growing economic uncertainty were forcing countries to rethink their dependencies, diversify supply chains and prioritise trusted partnerships over cost and efficiency, ANI reported.Jaishankar identified repeated shocks to the international system as the first defining feature, saying decades of steady globalisation had been disrupted by a series of crises, including the Covid-19 pandemic, major conflicts, trade disruptions and economic volatility."Let's start with the current state of the world. To my mind, it has five defining features," he said, identifying the first as "the shocks to the international system".He said the global order, which had evolved steadily through globalisation over several decades, was now facing successive disruptions that had exposed vulnerabilities in the interconnected international system.The second feature, according to Jaishankar, was the growing weaponisation of resources, energy, technology, market access and finance, with countries increasingly using their control over critical economic assets to advance strategic interests."Whether it is resources or energy, market access or technology, or indeed even finance, every aspect of global economic activity has been more and more openly weaponised by relevant players," he said.He added that physical and virtual chokepoints were also becoming instruments of strategic competition, warning that established international rules and assumptions were weakening.The remarks point to a changing international environment in which economic interdependence is increasingly being used as a source of geopolitical leverage. Control over critical resources, technology networks, financial systems and strategic trade routes can give countries the ability to influence or restrict the choices available to others.The third defining feature, he said, was the growing mindset of extreme competition and greater risk-taking. Jaishankar said countries were increasingly willing to take bigger risks in an attempt to convert their strategic advantages into concrete outcomes across different domains.The fourth feature was de-risking and diversification, which he described as natural responses to growing global uncertainty. He said major economies were reassessing their dependence on concentrated supply chains and seeking alternative sources of essential goods and resources."Our choices are shaped now less by cost and efficiency, and perhaps more dependent on reliability and multiplicity. New supply chains and new economic arrangements are starting to come into being," Jaishankar said.He added that the risks of over-concentration were increasingly being recognised, with countries either looking for alternatives or seeking ways to mitigate their exposure to disruptions.The fifth feature was the growing importance of trusted partnerships. Jaishankar said governments and businesses were placing greater value on reliable partners and shorter supply chains as they navigated an increasingly uncertain international environment."In such uncertain times, nations, as indeed enterprises, put a much greater value on trusted partners and shorter supply chains," he said.He also cautioned against the manipulation of international rules to disadvantage countries that abide by them, saying governments were becoming increasingly aware of how such rules could be used to advance strategic interests.Turning to India-Japan relations, Jaishankar called for deeper cooperation amid the changing global landscape, urging Japan to recognise India's transformation since 2014.He highlighted India's infrastructure growth, expanding domestic market and improvements in human resource development, calling for greater collaboration in semiconductors, critical minerals, advanced manufacturing, clean energy, pharmaceuticals and defence.Saying India and Japan had maintained friendly relations without any clash of interests, he expressed confidence in stronger ties under Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi."By expanding India-Japan ties, we will not only serve to stabilise and secure the Indo-Pacific but also add an important pillar to an increasingly multi-polar Asia and the world," he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Couple ordered to cut hedge after claiming it was not a hedge
articles.summary: They insisted the description of the boundary plants was wrong and instead claimed it was a mixture of 17 closely planted trees and shrubs.
articles.body:
A couple has been ordered to reduce the size of their hedge after they claimed it was not a hedge at all.

Prof Angus Macdonald and Dr Patricia Macdonald received a notice from East Lothian Council after neighbours complained the trees and shrubs were overhanging onto their property, shedding branches, leaves and berries, and blocking out the sky.

The couple appealed to Scottish ministers and insisted the description of the boundary plants was wrong, claiming it was actually a mixture of 17 closely planted trees and shrubs.

But the Scottish government reporter stated the plants met the definition of a high hedge in Scotland and ruled in favour of the council.

In Scotland, a high hedge is defined as a row of two or more trees and shrubs which are taller than two metres above the ground.

The reporter said: "I am satisfied the shrubs and trees are a high hedge, which acts as a barrier to light and prevents the reasonable enjoyment of the neighbouring property."

The council ordered for it to be cut down and maintained at a maximum height of 2.5m (8ft) but excluded an ash and willow tree at either end of the boundary wall from any work.

More stories from Edinburgh, Fife & East

In the appeal, the couple said the trees and ivy made a "significant contribution" to the visual amenity of the street which sits within the Musselburgh Conservation Area.

They said the structure of the trees and shrubs provides shelter from extreme weather, cleans the air of pollutants and helps to reduce high temperatures during summer.

"It has also provided considerable support for wildlife of every kind, including more than 50 species of birds, more than 10 species of butterflies and numerous species of bees and other useful insect pollinators," the couple added.

The reporter said the hedge would continue to contribute at a lower height.

They ordered the time to comply with high hedge notice be expanded to ensure it could be met outside of bird nesting season.

articles.title: 'Good for the people' if politicians stopped doing media, says secretary of state
articles.summary: Sir Chris Bryant said all that "talking to the media emphasises the divisions rather than the collaborations".
articles.body:
The secretary of state for Northern Ireland has said that if politicians stayed off the media for a month it would "probably be very good for the people".

Sir Chris Bryant said it breaks his heart that because of the crisis over agreeing a budget he can't get round to issues like violence against women and girls, or resolving community tensions.

He told a committee of MPs that was "one of the symbols of the kind of complete abnormality that now seems to pervade Northern Ireland politics".

Ministers on the Stormont executive say they can't strike a budget without additional money from the Treasury .

The government has offered around £1.5 billion in extra funding over the next three years but ministers say they need more.

It means Northern Ireland faces the prospect of strikes by public sector workers because there is no way of meeting pay claims.

Asked by the committee chair Tonia Antoniazzi how much money ministers required he said: "Oh I mean it changes every week. One version is another billion pounds."

He added that some politicians "won't sit in the same room as each other".

He told members of the Northern Ireland Affairs Committee: "The point is that Northern Ireland is getting fair funding, and whatever the envelope is, if you were a councillor, you would have to set a legal budget.

"You just have to make the sums add up. And what really frustrates, I think, all of us is, I've tried processes of adjudicating between the different parties, because let's face it, the parties aren't talking to each other at the moment."

"I mean, I think it's a very odd system where you have a series of meetings with different political parties, and they all go out and do a press conference beforehand, and they basically say 'I'm going to tell him what's what" and then afterwards they have another press conference in which they say 'I told him what's what', that isn't a way to negotiate.

"It turns all the politicians into Northern Ireland into commentators on politics rather than actually players making decisions.

"But I would actually also add that I think sometimes all that talking to the media emphasises the divisions rather than the collaborations.

"And if everybody switched off the media, didn't go on anything for a month, it will probably be very good for the people of Northern Ireland."

He said the crisis "really must make us all think long and hard about whether we have the right structures and institutions in Northern Ireland, and that takes us back to a very big discussion in relation to the way everything was set up back in the Good Friday Agreement and then in the St Andrews Agreement.

"Does a lot of this need review now? And when we, I think, if we get to the 30th anniversary of the Good Friday Agreement, and we haven't done some radical surgery, we will think that that is that we are failing our citizens in Northern Ireland," he said.

articles.title: Before the first bullet: Army rescued 27 from seminary, then hunted LeT terrorist Lateef Bhat
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Security forces evacuated 27 people from Darul Uloom, an educational institution next to the mosque where top Lashkar-e-Taiba commander
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Security forces evacuated 27 people from Darul Uloom, an educational institution next to the mosque where top Lashkar-e-Taiba commander Mohammad Lateef Bhat was holed up. The evacuation took place before security forces launched an encounter against Lateef in Zangalpora village of Jammu and Kashmir’s Kulgam district on Wednesday.According to officials, an officer from the Army's 9 Rashtriya Rifles volunteered to enter the adjoining seminary along with his buddy and safely evacuate 25 girl students and two teachers.Once the civilians were moved to a safe spot, troops of the 9 Rashtriya Rifles and the Special Operations Group of the Jammu and Kashmir Police launched the final assault and fired tear gas into the mosque to smoke out the terrorist.Officials asserted that the troops maintained a tight cordon to prevent his escape and exercised maximum restraint to ensure that the religious structure suffered no damage.Northern Army Commander Lt Gen Pratik Sharma, General Officer Commanding-in-Chief, met troops in South Kashmir after the successful conclusion of the operation.How security forces tracked down Lateef BhatAccording to officials, a search party accompanied by local civilians entered the mosque following specific intelligence inputs. They found a room on the top floor locked from the inside.When security personnel asked the occupant to come out, he opened fire, confirming that Bhat was inside. The Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) terrorist carried a cash reward of Rs 15 lakh on his head.Senior Army officers in South Kashmir were determined not to let Bhat escape the cordon this time. He had earlier managed to flee during an encounter in Shopian on July 8, in which another terrorist, Zakir, was killed.The operation followed a November 11 attack on a CRPF picket in Kulgam by Bhat and his associate Umar Nasir Dar, which left three personnel injured. Security forces subsequently launched extensive cordon and search operations across Kulgam and neighbouring Shopian and Anantnag districts.Around 2,000 personnel from the Army, Special Operations Group (SOG) and CRPF were deployed for grid-based searches, backed by a Mobile Bunker Command Post (MBCP)."Since November 11, cordon and search operations have been underway. In certain areas, it took us nearly three days to complete the searches due to high population density," a senior officer said.He added that although the operations may have caused some inconvenience to residents, there had been no complaints of excesses by security personnel.Bhat, who was in his early 20s, had passed school and previously worked as a carpenter. He went missing in November 2025 before joining LeT and its offshoot, The Resistance Front (TRF).According to security agencies, he was the prime suspect in several terror incidents in South Kashmir, including the killing of India Reserve Police head constable Ashiq Hussain Qureshi in Anantnag on July 22 and the targeted killing of two non-local labourers from Chhattisgarh in Kulgam on July 31.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Jordan Parke 'unbothered' when BBL woman collapsed, inquest told
articles.summary: Alice Webb died in 2024 after having a procedure known as a Brazilian Butt Lift, an inquest hears.
articles.body:
A man who carried out a cosmetic procedure which an expert said led to a woman's death seemed "unbothered" when paramedics arrived to help her, an inquest has heard.

Mother-of-five Alice Webb, 33, collapsed at a friend's house in Gloucester on 23 September 2024 and died the following day after having a Brazilian Butt Lift (BBL).

Jordan Parke, who police said they had "no doubt" carried out the procedure, was under investigation for gross negligence manslaughter when he died in 2026.

Earlier an expert pathologist told the inquest, which is taking place in front of a jury at Gloucestershire Coroner's Court, that a "gel-like" liquid was found in blood vessels in Webb's brain, lungs, and heart.

Could you live under deep-sea pressure for 28 days?

How to reduce fire risks at home this Christmas

Hosepipe ban lifted after rain refills reservoirs

Webb, from Wotton-under-Edge, had been given a non-surgical BBL shortly before collapsing.

Surgical BBLs involve inserting silicone-filled implants and/or removing fat from other parts of the body before injecting it into the buttocks, while non-surgical BBLs involve injecting dermal filler into the buttocks.

During the jury inquest at Gloucestershire Coroner's Court on Wednesday, Dr Stephen Leadbeatter, a Home Office forensic pathologist, said he considered her cause of death to be "embolisation of hyaluronic acid from introduction into buttocks".

Embolisation is when something is carried in the bloodstream from one part of the body to another. Hyaluronic acid was the filler used in the procedure.

Katy Skerrett, senior coroner for Gloucestershire, told the inquest an ambulance had been called at about 21:00 BST on the day Webb collapsed. Despite resuscitation attempts, she died in hospital during the early hours of the next day.

Allanah Kingston, a paramedic for South West Ambulance Service who responded to the 999 call, said Webb was snoring and unable to manage her airway - in which vomit was stuck - and her blood pressure became low and unreadable.

An ECG showed massive ischemia, "which showed part of heart was dying; we knew it was not good," Kingston added, before Webb went into cardiac arrest.

She told the inquest Parke and a woman present named Jemma - whose address Alice received the liquid BBL at - appeared "unbothered by the situation" and demonstrated a "lack of understanding that the treatment may have caused illness".

During a post-mortem examination on 26 September 2024, Leadbeatter noted several dressings on each upper thigh and base of each buttock, which he assumed were covering "injection sites".

Skerrett told jurors Parke - known as the "Lip King" - had died "at a later stage".

Parke, 34, lived in Manchester, where he ran a salon from his home address, and had a large social media following.

He was under investigation for gross negligence manslaughter but died earlier this year, meaning the criminal case was unable to proceed, Det Insp Adam Stacey, from Gloucestershire Constabulary, told the inquest.

Det Insp Stacey said he had "no doubt" in his mind Parke, who had received no professional medical training, conducted the procedure Alice underwent shortly before her death, given the video evidence.

Of Parke's certificates found in Manchester, "none of them showed any degree of reassurance in degree of their formality", he added.

A number of procedures had been carried out by Parke, who, in 2023, had been subject to investigation by Dudley environmental health officers, who issued him with a prohibition notice to not perform BBL procedures.

Concerns regarding basic first aid, lack of lifesaving equipment, and the use of anesthesia without prescription had also been raised, and another prohibition notice was issued to Parke in Salford in 2024.

He was not registered with the General Medical Council or the General Pharmaceutical Council, and the products he used were unlicensed in the UK. He also lacked a medical prescribing certificate.

Leadbeatter said he had not found any indication of clots blocking Webb's lungs, but did find a "gel-like material" in the fatty tissue and within muscle of her buttocks. It was also present in nearby nerves.

The material was also found in blood vessels elsewhere in the body, he said.

"I saw it in lungs, also within the section of the buttocks, and in small blood vessels in parts of the brain, in the heart and in small blood vessels in the thyroid gland and kidney," Leadbeatter told the jury.

He added there had been no evidence of an allergic reaction and a toxic pathology test found nothing in the blood that could explain Webb's death.

Webb had her own business - Crystal Clear Aesthetics - in Wotton-under-Edge.

Morgan Louise Townsend, Alice's sister-in-law, became tearful as she spoke at the inquest, and said she spoke to Alice every day.

When asked if Webb had paid for the treatment, she said: "She'd paid for the course but she had to pay Jordan £2,300 for the procedure he did on her."

Townsend said Webb had seemed "absolutely fine that day", and had kept her updated with pictures and videos throughout the treatment.

"At 19:31, she sent me photo of the filler that was going to go in her, I was shocked at how much there was," Townsend said.

"[Parke] said he was giving her 400ml for free, in total 1,400ml. She sent messages and said 'OMG it kills'."

Townsend added Webb sent a video of Parke giving her the treatment.

The last message from Webb to Townsend came at 20:12, she told the inquest, and consisted of just one word: "Painful".

articles.title: ‘Crimea is turning into an island’: How Ukraine hit Putin’s prized bridge
articles.summary: A weeks-long operation was behind two waves of strikes using long-range missiles and drones developed in Ukraine.
articles.body:
It was a symbolic blow for Moscow and a sign of Kyiv’s growing tactical and technological prowess.

The Ukrainian military had worked for weeks to knock out Russian air defence systems, radars and drone jamming equipment guarding the only bridge that links southern Russia to Crimea.

On Tuesday, it launched two precision attacks on the crossing with heavy drones and cruise missiles. One of the bridge’s arches collapsed, blocking the movement of cars and limiting the movement of trains to one track, while about 200 metres (660 feet) of the tarmac was heavily damaged and submerged.

“Logistically speaking, Crimea is turning into an island,” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevych told Al Jazeera.

According to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, drones developed by Kyiv hit the bridge at night, while Ukrainian Neptune missiles were among the weapons that targeted the rail section. Ukrainian-made Flamingo missiles were also involved in the operation, he said.

Netherlands-based company Destinus told the Reuters news agency that seven of its Ruta cruise missiles hit the bridge during the multistage operation.

The arch fell into the deepest part of the Kerch Strait, preventing the passage of freighters bringing grain and steel from southwestern Russia or occupied Ukrainian regions.

The blockade will further deprive Russian farmers of the ability to ship their grain to the Black Sea and beyond, including the Mediterranean – and could lead to an increase in global grain prices.

But many in Ukraine are adamant that the Kremlin is deaf to the woes of Russian farmers and businessmen.

Russian President Vladimir Putin “doesn’t care about their pockets”, Taras, a drone pilot in eastern Ukraine, told Al Jazeera. “No matter how much their economy is destroyed, he knows they’ll keep mum and suffer through.”

“Putin’s biggest problem is that he still can’t fathom how technologically advanced we have become,” Taras said, withholding his last name in accordance with wartime protocol.

Zelenskyy called the sting “unprecedented” and its execution “flawless”.

The Kremlin accused the “neo-Nazi junta” in Kyiv of escalating the war.

“The Kyiv regime keeps striking civilian targets,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday.

“There is no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than before,” he said the next day, adding that Moscow is determined to “continue the hostilities”.

The Crimean bridge embodies the crowning achievement of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s leadership – the Black Sea peninsula’s “return” to Russia in 2014.

The 19km (12 mile) double-arched lacework of steel and concrete cost $3.8bn and opened in 2018, four years after Crimea’s annexation.

The bridge links Crimea to Russia by straddling the Kerch Strait that divides the Sea of Azov from the Black Sea. Kyiv has long denounced its construction as “illegal”.

Each arch is 227 metres (745 feet) long and weighs thousands of tonnes. They were assembled, welded and painted with anti-corrosion coating onshore, before crews operating giant, floating construction cranes installed them on top of the bridge.

Only the Syvash, a labyrinth of lagoons, salt marshes and wetlands known as the Rotten Sea, divides Crimea from southern Ukraine. Just three strips of land were wide and firm enough for the road and rail link that has become a symbol of Russia’s hold over Crimea.

The bridge also served as a major transport hub for millions of tourists and tens of thousands of Russian troops who invaded southern Ukraine in 2022.

The attack coincided with Putin’s trip to Shenzhen in southern China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, where he is due to hold a three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and United States President Donald Trump.

The destruction of the arch has gone unreported in Russian media, which described the damage as “insignificant”, causing “temporarily delayed trains”.

While many Ukrainians have celebrated the operation and posted viral memes of the attack, foreign observers offer a more sober analysis.

“There’s been practically no movement [of military personnel or supplies along the bridge] for a year, only occasional gas trucks in columns,” Nikolay Mitrokhin, a researcher at Germany’s Bremen University, told Al Jazeera.

He said Zelenskyy should have commissioned more mid-range drones to block roads in occupied Ukrainian regions along the Sea of Azov, where Russian supply trucks still move at “relatively low risk”. Instead, Mitrokhin explained, resources were focused on the Kerch Bridge because Zelenskyy was fixated on destroying it.

“In the military sense, the [attack] was counterproductive,” he said.

Russia has been attacking bridges in Ukraine, with equally devastating results.

On Tuesday, Russian drones and missiles damaged two of the five bridges across the Dnipro River that divides the Ukrainian capital.

Previous attacks on the crossings paralysed road and subway traffic, and Kyiv residents now spend hours in huge traffic jams.

Bridges in four more Ukrainian regions have also been damaged or destroyed in recent Russian strikes.

The attacks are part of Moscow’s new strategy to destroy the pillars of the Ukrainian economy, according to Kyiv-based analyst Aleksey Kushch.

“While in the past, mostly the sites of infrastructure, logistics [and] energy generation were on the strike list, these days the list of targets has extended to include hypermarket chains, mining companies, processing plants and many more sites,” he told Al Jazeera.

The aim of the military campaign is to create an “empty economic space” that would decimate Ukraine’s gross domestic product (GDP), the number of jobs and the amount of tax revenue, he said.

articles.title: ‘Status quo’ between US and Iran could break out into war, analysts warn
articles.summary: Iran and the US have continued to exchange strikes in recent days, but all-out war has so far been avoided.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Iranian forces have targeted military bases in Bahrain and Kuwait as the United States has hit military and radar installations in southern Iran after a spate of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Both the US and Iran appear reluctant for all-out conflict again, as happened during the opening weeks of the war, which the US and Israel began on February 28. But analysts said the current situation is inherently unstable and could potentially escalate again into full-blown war that could see Israel rejoin the strikes on Iran.

US forces are deployed at military bases in Bahrain and Kuwait, which Tehran considers complicit in the recent strikes on southern Iran. The two countries had not been attacked since early September, but both have been targeted by Iranian drones in recent days.

The lull for Bahrain ended on November 13 when Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) directed explosive-laden drones towards the Riffa Air Base after US air strikes in Sirik, a port on Iran’s Hormozgan coast. Several more Iranian strikes have followed, and the US has also attacked Iran’s Qeshm Island on multiple occasions.

After hitting Bahrain, the IRGC warned Manama against its security partnership with the US and its treatment of Shia Muslim leaders after several were recently given lengthy prison sentences.

Kuwait reported incoming drones overnight into Wednesday. Iran’s military said it was targeting US equipment at Ali Al Salem Air Base, including missile launch platforms. No Iranian missiles were used against Bahrain or Kuwait, unlike attacks earlier in the war, according to reports.

Mohammad Eslami, a Tehran-based foreign policy analyst, said Iran aims to gradually degrade US military assets across the region, particularly those Tehran believes were active during the war.

“So long as the war does not end in a political agreement, Iran will continue to do this, regardless of other factors like the blockade,” he told Al Jazeera.

US President Donald Trump and senior officials in his administration have insisted a naval blockade on southern Iranian ports and tough sanctions against Tehran are working. These appear designed to either force Iran to concede to US demands for ending the war or lead to the collapse of its government.

But Tehran is increasingly signalling that it will not accept a continuation of the status quo as the sanctions are severely impacting imports and exports to Iran. The Iranian military’s targeting of regional military facilities this week is likely related to this US economic embargo, said Andreas Krieg, an associate professor in security studies at King’s College London.

“The strikes on Bahrain and Kuwait are about probing American red lines, testing how far Tehran can push the boundaries of military confrontation without triggering another full-scale war,” Krieg told Al Jazeera.

“By targeting American assets in Gulf states, Iran is trying to make Washington’s economic warfare increasingly costly for its regional partners.”

The US military’s Central Command says its maritime blockade has prevented Iran from loading any crude oil onto its tankers since late August. It has also claimed more than 1.7 billion barrels of crude have been shipped through the Strait of Hormuz by Iran’s Arab neighbours under US protection and in defiance of demands for vessels to use a route Tehran has authorised.

Iran continues to sell oil stored outside the blockade limits to China, although at reduced levels.

The IRGC maintains that the strait remains closed to unauthorised transit and continues to target the oil shuttle system, which it believes is run primarily by the United Arab Emirates . This relay system has succeeded in getting more energy exports out of the Gulf using tankers that transfer their cargoes to other ships that deliver the oil to global markets.

The UAE’s state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) confirmed on Wednesday that one of its vessels was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz and one crew member was missing.

To reopen the strategic waterway, Tehran has demanded the US lift its blockade and an Iran-Oman deal outlining coordinated transit routes in the strait be honoured along with other carefully sequenced US concessions on lifting the sanctions on Iran and releasing its frozen assets.

Mediators like Qatar and Pakistan continue to try to bridge the gaps between the two sides, but the talks have largely reached an impasse as both sides refuse to budge on their main demands.

Eslami said Trump and his senior political and military officials have failed to adopt a clear strategy towards Tehran, particularly in light of Iran’s promise of a response across the region and beyond if attacked.

“The “Iron Gate” and other measures are effectively a pretty name for their indecision,” he said about the US plan to create overland trade disruptions . “The issue in the negotiations is that they don’t know what to do about the raised proposals due to the political costs they would have to pay in the US.”

Still, some Iranians appear to believe they are the dominant party in the current impasse. Speaking to state television on Wednesday, the IRGC’s political deput,y Yadollah Javani, said Trump was stuck in a “quagmire” and must accept defeat.

“Trump has no choice but to accept realities in the field,” he said, adding that Iran was upgrading its arsenal and prepared for another major outbreak in fighting with the US.

After a third US aircraft carrier strike group entered the Arabian Sea, Iran’s army chief, Amir Hatami, said the armed forces were prepared for any new attacks by Washington.

“The enemy is preparing its forces, but the army and other armed forces monitor their movements vigilantly,” he said in a speech on Wednesday. “The preparedness of armed forces increases by the moment. Our response to any error by the enemy and its backers will be more decisive than before.”

Trump’s administration appears split on how to handle Iran with hawks such as Defense Secretary Pete Hesgeth reportedly wanting a more forceful approach to Tehran.

Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, said others believe Washington can maintain the blockade and economic pressure indefinitely while avoiding full-scale war. But the latest attacks demonstrate the difficulty of maintaining such an arrangement.

“Beyond the risk of unintended escalation, the longer the blockade and economic pressure campaigns continue, the greater the incentive for Tehran to deliberately escalate in an attempt to break the deadlock by force,” he wrote in an analysis online.

Krieg said he expects Tehran to intensify calibrated pressure through attacks on US military assets and by continuing to target vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

This strategy could also potentially press the Iran-allied Houthis, the Yemeni armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), to make further advances along the Bab al-Mandeb strait , another strategic chokepoint for maritime trade and global energy supplies.

“But this equilibrium is inherently unstable. If diplomacy fails to produce tangible economic relief, I believe further escalation will become increasingly likely,” Krieg said. “The greatest danger is that both sides keep pushing each other’s thresholds until one crosses a red line neither fully understood.”
